justice: Both sides of the street have paved sidewalks of similar width, suggesting a relatively even allocation of pedestrian space.
Street lighting poles, road markings, and maintained sidewalks indicate that public infrastructure is distributed consistently along the corridor rather than concentrated on one side only.
Accessibility is only moderate because no curb ramps, tactile paving, or other barrier-free details are clearly visible at the intersection ahead from this viewpoint.
safety: The roadway has clear centerline and edge line markings, which help organize vehicle movement and reduce ambiguity for all road users.
A marked crosswalk is visible ahead, providing a designated pedestrian crossing point.
Tall streetlights are installed on both sides of the street, supporting visibility and perceived safety, although daytime conditions prevent judging nighttime performance fully.
livability: The street appears clean and orderly, with well-maintained pavement, aligned light poles, and trimmed roadside trees, which supports basic environmental quality.
However, the corridor feels low in street activity, with very few visible pedestrians, storefronts, or active ground-floor uses contributing to social vibrancy.
Large building setbacks and fenced edges on the right side create a more institutional and less interactive street edge, limiting everyday street life.
sustainability: Rows of street trees on both sides provide some green infrastructure and long-term environmental benefits.
Wide sidewalks create conditions that can support walking as a low-carbon travel mode.
Sustainability is limited by the absence of visible dedicated bicycle lanes, bus stops, or rainwater-management features such as bioswales or permeable planting strips.
aesthetics: The street has a strong sense of order created by straight alignment, consistent lamp posts, and neat lane markings.
Young street trees and landscaped edges soften the corridor and improve the visual character compared with a fully hardscaped street.
Visual appeal is weakened somewhat by the overcast sky, blanker building edges on the left, and limited facade variety at street level.
comfort: Physical comfort is supported by smooth asphalt on the roadway and even, paved sidewalks that appear free of clutter.
Thermal comfort is only moderate because the trees are still relatively small and provide limited shade coverage across the sidewalks.

Psychological comfort benefits from the low traffic volume and uncluttered street space, but the broad roadway and sparse human activity can make the environment feel somewhat exposed and less socially buffered.
walkability: Sidewalks are continuous on both sides and appear sufficiently wide for ordinary pedestrian movement.
A marked crosswalk is visible ahead, improving route continuity across the street.
Walkability is constrained by limited shade from small trees, low frontage activity, and no clearly visible pedestrian amenities such as benches or refuge features.
bikeability: There is no clearly marked or protected bicycle lane visible on the roadway, which substantially reduces cycling support.
The street appears relatively calm and wide, which may allow informal cycling, but cyclists would still need to share space with motor vehicles.
No visible bicycle parking, bike boxes, or dedicated cycling markings are present to improve convenience or reduce conflict at the intersection ahead.
